prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency.

statement.case_for: I keep B005 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and the exchange has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The deciding criterion for me is the one the prize statutes use: a discovery or invention, with the people who are responsible for the original work. The lattice clock passes on both counts. The invention is a single idea, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, and it was followed by a realization at about 1e-18 that several laboratories on different continents have reproduced and surpassed. Its systematics are understood and it is already used for tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. Attribution fits two seats with a clear conceptual originator and a clear performance leader, and all six B005 supporters independently proposed the same two names. The chair asked for an explicit criterion between B005 and B014. Mine is this: where two candidates both have a clear conceptual step and broad reproduction, I prefer the one whose record is longer and whose credit can be stated without leaving out a person who made the decisive step. B005 meets that test today; B014 may well meet it in a few years. I also want the citation kept to the lattice clock and not to precision timekeeping in general, which answers the chair's question about overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes: those honoured the comb and single-quantum-system control, and the lattice clock is a separate invention that they enabled and did not contain.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against is the one several of us recorded. The territory is adjacent to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, so a committee that reads precision measurement as one programme could judge a third prize redundant. The redefinition of the second has not occurred, so part of the impact is prospective, although I do not think an institutional decision should be the test of a discovery. The credit rests on recollection, not on verified sources: the exact priority between the Tokyo magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice spectroscopy and the Boulder strontium effort, the role of the Paris and PTB groups, and the ultrastable-laser contributors outside the pair are not settled by the supplied names. Finally, B014 has a wider effect on condensed-matter physics and a cleaner theory-plus-experiment story, and Kroll is right that it draws the broadest ranking support (eight of eight ranked it) and cannot be treated as a fallback.

responses.point: B014 is the only candidate ranked by all eight members, the 2011 continuum model followed by the 2018 discovery is an unusually clean theory-to-experiment line, and waiting will not improve the case.
responses.response: I take the second point seriously, and I agree that breadth of recognition is real evidence that the discovery is not idiosyncratic. Where we differ is on what waiting buys. The question the field has not answered, why the superconductivity appears, is exactly what would let the committee write a citation that survives later work, and sample variability from strain and disorder is still an active issue. I also do not think the omission of Yuan Cao is a small matter for an experimental prize built on the 2018 papers. You argue that the group leader is normally credited, and that is true, but the cut is arguable and a longer record would let us see which contributions stand. I also agree with you that the 2011 paper is a joint result by Bistritzer and MacDonald, so I would keep all three names if B014 were chosen. My preference for B005 comes from maturity and credit, not from doubting the physics of B014.

responses.point: The choice is between a measurement-science prize and a new-phenomenon prize, and a clock may be an instrument achievement and not a discovery about nature.
responses.response: I agree that this is the right framing, but I do not accept that an instrument achievement is outside the prize. The statutes say discovery or invention, and the lattice clock is an invention whose consequence is a quantitative change in what can be tested, not only a better number. Magic-wavelength trapping changes the statistical and systematic budget and made the 1e-18 regime reachable, and that is a conceptual step, not an incremental refinement. I would add one thing in your favour. Your move from B016 to B014 and your acceptance of Bistritzer as a joint author of the 2011 model are well argued, and I agree with you that if the committee wanted a new-phenomenon prize this year, B014 with three names is the defensible version. I simply weigh the decade of independent confirmation behind the clock more heavily than the speed of reproduction behind the moire work.

responses.point: Katori is credited with the concept and first strontium lattice spectroscopy and Ye with record accuracy and many-body effects, but fine priority between Tokyo and Boulder rests on recollection and should be checked, and B014 is a serious competitor.
responses.response: I agree on both points. On priority, I would make the final citation not claim more than the pair can carry: it should name the invention and its realization and should not say who was first. If the committee later finds that other groups (Paris, PTB) share the decisive step, the right response is a narrower citation, not a larger list, because the three-person limit and the credit are the constraint. I also accept your concession that B014 is not a fallback. Where I differ slightly from your emphasis is on ultrastable lasers: I regard them as enabling technology that is outside this ballot, and I would not try to resolve that by widening the credit.

responses.point: The prize would partly honour a precision-measurement programme whose headline payoff has not yet happened, and the citation should be kept from blurring ion clocks and lattice clocks.
responses.response: I accept the second concern fully and have changed the wording of my citation to name magic-wavelength trapping so that it stays with the lattice clock and does not extend to ion clocks that reach comparable accuracy by another route. On the first, I still hold that realized use in constants tests and geodesy is the relevant evidence, and the redefinition is an institutional step. I note that your bare citation is shorter than mine, and I would prefer the version that includes the mechanism, because it protects against the overlap concern you and Danielsson both raised.

responses.point: A committee that wants conceptual novelty rather than ever-better precision could judge the lattice clock incremental, and B014 would then deserve to outrank it.
responses.response: That is a fair test and I think the clock passes it, because the key step was a design idea (the magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between atom number and Doppler or recoil shifts), and nature was not asked a better question by tightening an existing one. I would not claim it surprised us in the way the 2018 experiments did. If the committee decides novelty about nature is the deciding criterion this year, I would accept B014 with all three names, and I think that is an honest statement of where the disagreement lies. It is not a disagreement about the quality of the science.

uncertainties: Whether priority among the early magic-wavelength proposals and the first lattice-clock demonstrations, and the roles of the Paris, PTB and other strontium and ytterbium groups, change the two-name credit; this rests on recollection and is not verified from the supplied material.
Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which I believe it is but which several members record as a reservation.
Whether B014 should outrank B005 on breadth of impact and ranking support, and how much weight the unsettled superconducting mechanism and the eight-year record deserve.
statement.conflict_note: My opening first choice was B051 (aberration-corrected electron optics), which is close to my own field of transmission electron microscopy and to the international microscopy community I lead. I have not advanced it in either round and would step back from any decision on it; it is not in my preferred configuration or my alternatives. I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and my Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson has no apparent link to B005 or B014 in my profile. My field proximity to B005 and B014 is only that of an experimentalist in materials physics.
